intro: Devoxx Belgium 2026 was mostly about working with coding agents: about a third of the sessions sat in the agentic engineering track, and most asked less what agents can do than how to check, review and contain them. The Java platform team showed a runtime that keeps getting leaner and faster, from compact object headers (on by default in JDK 27, speakers said) to Leyden's AOT cache and Valhalla value classes. Architecture and people talks argued for clear boundaries and for keeping the skills that AI makes easy to skip.

trends.title: The harness outweighs the model
trends.body: Several speakers said the system around an agent decides results more than the model does. Darwish cited Terminal-Bench, where the same Claude Opus 4.5 scored differently per harness. Rules in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md proved unreliable: Podlesniuk saw one of three runs ignore a word-for-word rule, and Petruzalek watched an agent edit a blocking hook script. The fix shown repeatedly was executable checks (ArchUnit, Error Prone, Maven Enforcer, OpenRewrite) whose failure messages become the agent's context. Speakers split on tooling: Grall and Charrière favoured plain CLIs and bash over MCP, while Ward and Tzolov's eval had an MCP docs server answer in 19 seconds against 318 for a shell agent.
trends.consensus: The harness around an agent shapes results more than the model does, and rules that matter belong in executable checks, not in CLAUDE.md prose.

debate.question: Should coding agents reach tools through MCP servers or plain CLIs?

sides.stance: CLIs and bash are lighter. Grall said agents increasingly prefer CLIs like gh over MCP servers; Charrière replaced a catalogue of tools with one bash tool, since every tool description eats a small model's context.

MCP pays off for current documentation. In Ward and Tzolov's eval the javadocs.dev MCP arm answered in about 19 seconds, while a shell agent grepping jars took 318. Petruzalek keeps MCP mainly for always-current docs.

trends.title: Review is the new bottleneck
trends.body: Agents make code cheap, but speakers agreed human review time has not shrunk. Martignole described huge PRs and an $86,000 bill as Back Market grew to 350 engineers on Claude Code. Rentea wants a fresh-context, adversarial AI to review before any human does; Cavalcanti showed such a review confidently reporting a bug that did not exist. Rivas and Martinelli review a short spec or plan instead of a 5,000-line PR, and Lippert and Gavrilescu want tools that show changes at architecture level. Hoogendoorn's team has dropped pull requests and code review for pairing and trunk-based development, while Schrijver insisted that if you bring it to review, it is your code.
trends.consensus: Agents produce code faster than people can review it, so human attention has to move to smaller or higher-level units: specs, plans, phases or architecture views.

debate.question: How much human code review does agent-written code still need?

sides.stance: None as a separate step. Hoogendoorn's team at iBOOD dropped pull requests and code reviews; quality comes from pairing, trunk-based development and thousands of automated tests, at about 100 deploys a day.

Less over time, with AI reviewing first. Rentea wants a fresh-context adversarial AI before any human, then halving review after months of good PRs; Petruzalek's parallel review sub-agents replace much of her line-by-line review.

A human must still own it. Cavalcanti saw a fresh-context Claude review invent a bug; Gavrilescu stopped reviewing and found 20 copies of one button; Schrijver: if you bring it to review, it's your code.

trends.title: Treat coding agents as untrusted code
trends.body: Security speakers agreed that prompt injection cannot be fixed with prompts. Gross called a coding agent remote code execution by design. Moraes showed "treat as data" wrappers beaten by forged closing tags and cited AgentDojo attack success of 45.5% on Qwen3 4B and about 5% on GPT-5. Vermeer demoed poisoned MCP tool descriptions and hidden instructions in skills, and argued pinned versions beat approval prompts. The shared answer was isolation: microVM sandboxes rather than containers (Šelajev noted the Docker socket gives root), host allowlists, and credentials swapped in by a proxy so they never enter the sandbox. Mehmandarov kept tag sandwiching, paired with closing-tag detection and canary tokens.
trends.consensus: Prompt injection cannot be prevented reliably, so agents need deterministic limits outside the model: microVM sandboxes, host allowlists, server-scoped tools and credentials injected by a proxy.

debate.question: Are prompt-level defences against injection worth keeping at all?

sides.stance: No, they are only suggestions. Moraes showed "treat as data" wrappers beaten by forged closing tags, Gross said probabilistic security is no security, and Šelajev got a classifier to run a secret-stealing script.

Yes, as one layer. Mehmandarov keeps tag sandwiching with closing-tag detection, canary tokens and a cheap intent-classifier model, then backs them with deterministic Bean Validation because all of it stays probabilistic.

trends.title: AI-found CVEs force faster patching
trends.body: Several speakers said models now find vulnerabilities faster than teams patch them. According to Salm, frontier-model scanning found over 450 possible vulnerabilities in Spring since March, leading to more than 200 fixes; Cvetkovic said Spring fixed more CVEs in a few months of 2026 than in the previous 13 years. Belfius said reported vulnerabilities roughly doubled around Claude Mythos's release, and Semeteys noted curl ended its bug bounty under duplicate and fabricated reports. Advice converged: automate upgrades and tests, rank CVEs by reachability and exposure rather than CVSS (Finkelshtein: Spring4Shell only hits WAR deployments on standalone Tomcat), and meet the Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties, live since September 2026.
trends.consensus: AI-assisted research is finding vulnerabilities faster than before, so teams need automated upgrades and tests, and should rank CVEs by reachability and exposure rather than CVSS alone.

debate.question: Does the flood of AI-found vulnerabilities make software safer?

sides.stance: The findings are real and become fixes. Salm said frontier-model scanning found over 450 possible Spring vulnerabilities, leading to more than 200 fixes; Cvetkovic said Spring fixed more CVEs in months than in 13 years.

Volume is not security when human triage is the bottleneck. Semeteys credited Mozilla's 22 Claude-found Firefox bugs, but said duplicate and fabricated reports swamp security teams, and curl ended its bug bounty.

trends.title: The JVM gets leaner and faster
trends.body: Pressler's keynote argued that if AI makes syntax matter less, the runtime matters more; platform talks brought numbers. Speakers said compact object headers are the default in JDK 27; van Dijk and Przybyl saw a 10-million-object heap drop from about 190 MB to 114 MB, though Parlog said to measure decompression's CPU cost. Leyden's AOT cache took a Quarkus REST app from about 350 ms to 80 ms startup, with caveats on custom class loaders. JEP 401 value classes are planned as a preview in JDK 28 according to the speakers, but Paumard and Forax warned generic code loses scalarization and null-safety remains open. Structured concurrency, they said, is proposed as final in JDK 28.
trends.consensus: Upgrading the JDK brings real memory and startup gains with little or no code change, from compact object headers to Leyden's AOT cache, each with some caveats.

debate.question: Will Valhalla value classes close Java's memory-layout gap?

sides.stance: Pressler called array memory layout Java's remaining structural handicap against low-level languages, and said Valhalla removes it by flattening values based on declared intent rather than manual layout control.

Paumard and Forax measured limits: streams and other generic code lose scalarization to erasure, heap flattening stops at about 64 bits, small flattened arrays were slower than pointers, and null-safety stays unsolved.

trends.title: Java reaches native code and GPUs
trends.body: A cluster of talks used FFM, the Vector API and Project Babylon to run numeric and AI work in Java without JNI or Python. Fumero's Babylon-based HAT brought a tiled matrix multiply to 78 µs against 77 µs for cuTile Python. TornadoVM's jitLLM reported decode at 93% of llama.cpp, and Peterssen's 3.3 MB Quixotic jar runs 17 model families on the CPU. Speakers differed on how far pure Java goes: Peterssen said only matrix multiply needs native code, while Przybyl showed the Vector API's gain halving against a well-written scalar loop and noted Elasticsearch now calls a C++ kernel through FFM. Sevarac found packaging CUDA the hard part.
trends.consensus: FFM, the Vector API and Project Babylon now let Java run numeric and AI workloads near native speed, without JNI or a Python runtime.

debate.question: Can pure Java kernels match native code for AI workloads?

sides.stance: Nearly everywhere. Peterssen said only matrix multiply needs native code, with attention at full speed on the Vector API; Fumero's Babylon-based HAT tile kernel ran in 78 µs against 77 µs for cuTile Python.

Native libraries still win the hottest paths. Przybyl saw the Vector API's gain halve against a tuned scalar loop, and Elasticsearch now calls a C++ kernel through FFM; jitLLM sends prefill matrix multiplies to cuBLAS.

trends.title: Boundaries before services
trends.body: Architecture talks pushed back on service count as a goal. Klaver's Port of Rotterdam had more than 4.5 microservices per engineer and is consolidating into Spring Modulith services along event-storming boundaries; Hillaert argued bounded contexts need not map one-to-one to services. Van de Ven warned that hexagonal layers relocate dependencies rather than remove them, while Vandeperre and van der Meer used separate build modules and ArchUnit to keep agent-written code clean. On consistency, Trandafir, Zinck and Sulyz all started from the dual-write problem, then covered outbox or Debezium CDC (with heartbeats so Postgres WAL cannot fill the disk), sagas with idempotent compensations, and reconciliation as the final net.
trends.consensus: Good business boundaries matter more than service count, and consistency across boundaries needs explicit patterns: outbox or CDC, sagas with idempotent compensations, and reconciliation.

debate.question: Are hexagonal and clean-architecture layers worth their cost?

sides.stance: Only where change justifies them. Van de Ven said layers relocate dependencies rather than remove them, mappers cannot protect against dropped columns, and hexagonal adds distance that costs money when code rarely changes.

Yes, especially with agents writing code. Vandeperre and van der Meer refactored a vibe-coded app into a framework-free domain with ports and adapters, separate build modules and ArchUnit tests, so drift fails the build.

trends.title: From writing code to judging it
trends.body: Speakers agreed developer roles are shifting, not disappearing, but disagreed on what to hold on to. Clark and Rohrer traced "programmers will be unnecessary" predictions back to Fortran in 1956 and named de-skilling as the real risk. Rentea's keynote urged moves toward product, architecture or quality work and concluded that hand debugging no longer pays, while Cavalcanti cited Bainbridge's automation paradox: people who only monitor lose the skills for what cannot be automated. Schrijver cited measured gains of 5-15% and METR's finding that developers felt faster while being 19% slower. Debois and ING treated scaling as an enablement problem, with shared, reviewed skills and agents rather than individual habits.
trends.consensus: Developer roles are shifting toward specifying, judging and owning results rather than disappearing, and accountability for agent output stays with people.

debate.question: Should developers keep hands-on skills like debugging?

sides.stance: Let them go. Rentea said Claude found 17 memory leaks and 10 bottlenecks in 30 minutes, called hand debugging and tuning "unethical" at work, and set a target of over 95% generated code.

Keep them on purpose. Cavalcanti cited Bainbridge: people who only monitor automation lose the skills for what cannot be automated, so he still writes API shapes himself; Clark and Rohrer called de-skilling the real risk.
